In this lesson, you are introduced to the concept of communication systems and signal processing.
INTRODUCTIONM
Communication systems convey information (voice, music, video, code) from one point to another.
Every time you turn on a radio or television set, you are using a communication system.
Signal processing is how the information is changed from one form to another in communication systems.
Even a small hand held radio uses signal processing. The signals in the air must be changed to audio signals.
However, before you perform your first laboratory experiment in signal processing, you need to know some safety rules.

COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS
This course teaches signal processing. Since all communication systems use signal processing, let's discuss a basic communication system.
DISCUSSION
A communication system conveys information, or intelligence, from a source to a destination.
All communication systems consist of a transmitter, transmission medium and a receiver.
The purpose of the transmitter is to convert Input Information to an electrical signal or an electromagnetic wave - signal processing.
For example, a telephone changes your voice to voltage levels that are suitable for sending over wires.
A radio station changes music from tapes or records to electromagnetic waves that are suitable for sending over the air ways.
The operation of the transmitter depends on what type of information is going to be sent.

Now that you are familiar with a basic communication system, let's look at two limitations.
BANDWIDTH NOISE
The first limitation is bandwidth, which is the information carrying capacity of the system.
All communication circuits contain components that are frequency sensitive.
The reactance or frequency cut off points of these components limit the range of frequencies that pass through communication circuits.
In other words, communication circuits can only operate in a certain range of frequencies. The range is the bandwidth of the circuit or system.
The information, or intelligence, which is processed by a communication system must be in the bandwidth of the communication circuits.
This limits the amount or type of information that a communication system can process.
For example, the range of frequencies that your voice produces is between approximately 40 and 4,000 Hz - a bandwidth of
Consequently, early telephone communication systems were designed to operate in a bandwidth of 4 kHz.
However, when computer systems started to use telephone systems to communicate, problems arose because of limited bandwidth.
The information being sent from one computer to another used higher frequencies, so a bigger bandwidth was needed.
Communication system bandwidths can also distort some information signals.
For example, the bandwidth of a communication system that processes square waves must be large enough to include the odd harmonics of the fundamental frequency.
If not, then distortion of the information signal, square wave, occurs.

The second limiting factor of a communication system is noise.
Try communicating to a friend at a rock concert!...........
Seriously though, there are many types of noise that effect a communications system such as:
If the noise signals in a communication system are larger than the information signals, the information is lost.
The quality of a communication system is measured by its signal to noise ratio or S/N ratio.
The S/N ratio value is normally expressed in decibels (dB).
Noise can be reduced or eliminated in communications systems by: Graphic: Increasing Power Out Electronic Filters Shielding of Equipment
However, one type of noise is always present, thermal noise.
Thermal noise is caused by temperature variations in electronic components.
At any temperature above absolute zero, electrons exhibit random motion.
The random motion results in the generation of voltages or currents which cause noise.
No matter how carefully designed, all communication systems exhibit noise.
When the signal power is less than the noise power, the information is lost. Noise is a limitation in a communication system.
Communication circuits can eliminate all noise in a system.
Communication circuits can be designed to reduce or eliminate some types of noise but not all. Thermal noise can not be eliminated, it is due to the communication circuits themselves.

You have heard the word "Signal Processing" and probably have a general idea of what it is by now.
Technically, signal processing is the alteration of a signal in order to accomplish effective, efficient and reliable transmission and reception.
Signal processing includes:raphic:Amplification Filtering Reshaping Modulation & demodulation Multiplexing & demultiplexing
Amplification increases signals to a usable level for other signal processing and compensates for attenuation through the transmission medium.
Filtering of signals is used to reduce noise and to separate various signals from one another.
Reshaping of signals correct any pulse spreading or distortion of the information.
Modulation, demodulation and multiplexing, demultiplexing are different ways to combine and separate transmitted signals.

Let's briefly discuss Modulation and Demodulation..........
Modulation is a method of combining two different signals and is used in the transmitter section of a communication system.
Demodulation is the separating of the two signals and is used in the receiver section of a communication system.
One of the two signals is the modulation or intelligence signal. It is called the modulating signal.
The other signal is called a Carrier signal. It is used to carry the modulating signal through the transmission medium to the receiver.
The modulator circuit combines the two signals in the transmitter section of a communication system. A demodulator separates the signals in the receiver.
Modulator and demodulator circuits combine and separate signals in four basic ways. Graphic:Amplitude Frequency Phase Pulse
Sometimes Frequency and Phase Modulation are grouped together and are called Angle modulation.
When the modulation signal is used to change the carrier signal's amplitude it is called amplitude modulation, AM for short. This is where AM radio got its name.

When the modulation signal is used to change the frequency of the carrier signal according to the information signal amplitude it is called frequency modulation, FM for short. This is where FM radio got its name.

Phase modulation, called PM for short, changes the phase angle of the carrier signal as a function of the modulation signal. It is hard to show a signal that has phase modulation without showing frequency modulation. The phase changes in relation to the intelligence.
Notice the FM signal has the greatest frequency change at T1 and T3. This is when the modulating signal is peaked positive and negative.
Note that frequency cannot change without a phase change and phase cannot change without changing frequency.
The PM signal has the greatest frequency change at T0, T2 and T4 when the modulating signal phase is at the zero crossing point.
The only difference between FM and PM is that the modulated signal phase is shifted an entire 90 degrees.
Pulse modulation is a little different, the modulation signal is sampled. Pulse modulation is not continuous like AM, FM and PM.
Pulse modulation is used primarily in digital systems. There are various modulating methods.
Modulation has several advantages. aphic:* Efficient Transmission * Overcomes hardware assignment * Allows frequency assignment
Efficient transmissions are produced because a carrier frequency that best suits the circumstance can be chosen.

Hardware limitations can be overcome by choosing a carrier frequency that reduces the size of frequency sensitive components. For example: An antenna for audio frequencies would have to be 300 kM long. An antenna for the frequencies used in AM and FM radio is only about 1 meter.
Assigning different carrier frequencies allows more than one AM or FM radio station to be selected.

Multiplexing and demultiplexing are two other methods of signal processing.
Multiplexing is a method of combining several information signals into one signal in the transmitter section.
Demultiplexing is the separating of the one signal into the many signals in the receiver section.
Multiplexed signals can be used as a modulating signal for AM, FM or PM communication systems.
Multiplexer and demultiplexer circuits combine and separate signals in two basic ways.
Time division multiplexing samples each information input signal for a certain amount of time.
Between T0 and T1, information signal A is placed on the output line.
Between T1 and T2, information signal B is placed on the output line.
Between T2 and T3, signal A is again placed on the output line. Between T3 and T4, signal B is again used.
On the receiving end, the opposite happens. The received signal is divided into two signals.
Frequency Division Multiplexing uses modulators and a summation circuit.
Each information source is modulated with a different frequency.
Then the outputs of the modulators are summed.
The multiplexed signal sources are separated by filters and then the information signals are demodulated.
The advantage of multiplexing and demultiplexing is that many information sources can be transmitted on one channel or wire.
In fact, todays' telephone system allows 672 voice signals over a single telephone line.
